subject: chemistry
title: Transition metal chemistry
summary: d-block electron configurations and oxidation states, coordination complexes, ligands, coordination number and geometry, naming complexes, and how crystal field theory explains colour and magnetism.
body:
Transition metals such as iron, copper, cobalt and platinum sit in the d block. Their compounds colour gemstones, carry oxygen in our blood (iron in haemoglobin) and catalyse many synthetic reactions. Almost all of this behaviour comes from partly filled d orbitals and the way metals bond to surrounding molecules or ions called ligands.

## Think of it like this

### Coordination number is like counting hands on a tram pole, not people

On a crowded tram, several people may hold the same pole. Some hold on with one hand and some with two. A metal ion is like the pole, and each **ligand** is a person holding on: a **monodentate** ligand such as H₂O or NH₃ uses one "hand" (one **donor atom**), while a **bidentate** ligand such as ethane-1,2-diamine (en) uses two. The **coordination number** counts the hands on the pole, not the people — so [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has three ligands but a coordination number of 6. Someone holding on with both hands is much harder to dislodge, which is a little like the extra stability of the **chelate effect**.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the main reason chelates are so stable is entropy — one chelating ligand releases several monodentate ligands into solution — not just a stronger grip. Also, each "hand" is a **coordinate (dative) covalent bond**, in which the ligand provides both electrons.

### High spin and low spin are like choosing seats on a double-decker bus

Imagine a double-decker bus with three seats downstairs (the **t₂g** orbitals) and two seats upstairs (the **e_g** orbitals). People prefer a seat to themselves, but going upstairs means climbing the stairs. If the stairs are short (a small **crystal field splitting energy**, Δₒ, from **weak-field ligands**), newcomers would rather climb up than share a seat, giving a **high-spin** complex with as many unpaired electrons as possible. If the stairs are tall (a large Δₒ from **strong-field ligands** such as CN⁻), it is easier to share a seat downstairs — the cost of sharing is the **pairing energy**, P — giving a **low-spin** complex. That is why [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has 4 unpaired electrons but [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ has none.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* electrons don't "prefer" anything — the arrangement is simply whichever has the lower total energy, decided by comparing Δₒ with P — and real seat-sharing on a bus has no rule that the two people must have opposite spins.

### A complex's colour is like light through a coloured filter

When you look through coloured cellophane or a sunglasses lens, some colours of light are absorbed and you see what's left. A transition metal complex does the same: an electron absorbs visible light to jump from t₂g to e_g (a **d–d transition**), and the colour you see is the **complementary colour** of the light absorbed. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs mainly orange-red light, so it looks blue. Swapping the ligand changes the size of Δ, which changes which colour is absorbed — like changing to a different filter.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a filter is a fixed object, but in a complex the absorbed energy (Δ = hc ÷ λ) depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands — and d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions such as Zn²⁺ cannot absorb this way at all, so they are usually colourless.

### In real life

The iron in haemoglobin carries oxygen in your blood as a coordination complex, and the anticancer drug cisplatin is a square planar platinum complex. The colours of many gemstones come from small amounts of transition metal ions, and EDTA is used as a chelating agent in some foods and cleaning products to tie up metal ions.

## Key ideas

### Electron configurations of the d block

For the first row (Sc to Zn), the 4s orbital fills before 3d in the neutral atoms: for example, Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Exceptions: **Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹** and **Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹** (half-filled and filled d subshells are especially stable).

When transition metals form **cations**, the **4s electrons are removed first**, before any 3d electrons. Once electrons are in the 3d orbitals, the 3d level drops below 4s in energy. So:

- Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ (not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²)
- Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵
- Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹

A quick way to find the **d-electron count** of a first-row ion: d count = group number − oxidation state. For example, Co³⁺: group 9 − 3 = d⁶.

IUPAC defines a **transition element** as one with an incomplete d subshell in the atom or in at least one of its cations, so zinc (always d¹⁰ as Zn²⁺) is not one.

### Oxidation states

Transition metals show **variable oxidation states** because the 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost. Common examples: iron +2 and +3; copper +1 and +2; manganese from +2 (Mn²⁺) up to +7 (MnO₄⁻); chromium +3 and +6 (Cr₂O₇²⁻). High oxidation states usually occur in oxo-anions such as MnO₄⁻, which are often strong oxidising agents.

### Coordination complexes and ligands

A **coordination complex** contains a central metal atom or ion bonded to surrounding **ligands**. A ligand is a molecule or ion that donates a lone pair to the metal, forming a **coordinate (dative) covalent bond**. The ligand acts as a **Lewis base** and the metal as a **Lewis acid**.

The atom of the ligand that bonds to the metal is the **donor atom**. Ligands are classified by how many donor atoms they use:

| Type | Donor atoms | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Monodentate** | 1 | H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻, CO, OH⁻ |
| **Bidentate** | 2 | ethane-1,2-diamine (en), oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻) |
| **Polydentate** | 3 or more | EDTA⁴⁻ (hexadentate) |

Ligands with two or more donor atoms are **chelating ligands**: they grip the metal like a claw, forming a ring. Their complexes are extra stable — the **chelate effect** — mainly because one chelating ligand releases several monodentate ligands, raising entropy.

The complex is written in square brackets, with the overall charge outside: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Counter-ions sit outside the brackets, as in [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃.

To find the metal's oxidation state: overall charge = metal oxidation state + sum of ligand charges. In [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺, NH₃ is neutral and Cl⁻ is −1, so Co + (−1) = +2, giving **Co(+3)**.

### Coordination number and geometry

The **coordination number** is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal (not the number of ligands). In [Co(en)₃]³⁺ there are three ligands but six donor N atoms, so the coordination number is 6.

| Coordination number | Geometry | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | linear | [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ |
| 4 | tetrahedral | [CoCl₄]²⁻, [ZnCl₄]²⁻ |
| 4 | square planar (common for d⁸ ions) | [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [PtCl₂(NH₃)₂] |
| 6 | octahedral (most common) | [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺, [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ |

Square planar and octahedral complexes can show **cis–trans (geometric) isomerism**: in cis-[PtCl₂(NH₃)₂] (the anticancer drug cisplatin) the two Cl atoms are adjacent (90°); in the trans isomer they are opposite (180°). Octahedral complexes with three bidentate ligands, such as [Co(en)₃]³⁺, are chiral and exist as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (**optical isomers**).

### Naming coordination compounds

IUPAC rules (simplified):

1. Name the **cation before the anion**, as for any salt.
2. Within the complex, name **ligands first, in alphabetical order**, then the metal.
3. Use prefixes **di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-** for numbers of simple ligands (ignored when alphabetising). For ligands whose names already contain a number, such as ethane-1,2-diamine, use **bis-, tris-** and brackets.
4. Anionic ligands end in **-o**: chlorido (Cl⁻), cyanido (CN⁻), hydroxido (OH⁻), oxalato (C₂O₄²⁻). Neutral ligands: **aqua** (H₂O), **ammine** (NH₃, two m's), **carbonyl** (CO).
5. Give the metal's oxidation state in Roman numerals in brackets.
6. If the complex is an **anion**, the metal name ends in **-ate**, often using the Latin root: ferrate (Fe), cuprate (Cu), argentate (Ag), cobaltate, nickelate.

Examples:

- [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ — hexaaquacopper(II) ion
- [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ — pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
- K₃[Fe(CN)₆] — potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)

Older books use "chloro" and "cyano" instead of the current "chlorido" and "cyanido".

### Crystal field theory

**Crystal field theory** models ligands as negative point charges (or the negative ends of dipoles) approaching the metal. In a free ion the five d orbitals have equal energy. In an **octahedral** field, ligands approach along the x, y and z axes:

- The **d(z²)** and **d(x²−y²)** orbitals point directly at the ligands, so their electrons are repelled more. They rise in energy and are labelled **e_g**.
- The **d(xy), d(xz), d(yz)** orbitals point between the axes. They are lower in energy and labelled **t₂g**.

The energy gap between them is the **crystal field splitting energy**, Δₒ (o for octahedral). In a **tetrahedral** field the pattern is reversed (e below t₂) and the splitting is smaller, about 4/9 of Δₒ for the same metal and ligands.

The size of Δ depends on the metal ion (higher charge gives larger Δ) and on the ligand. Ligands are ranked in the **spectrochemical series**, from weak field (small Δ) to strong field (large Δ):

I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, en, CN⁻, CO (weakest to strongest field)

### High spin and low spin

For octahedral d⁴ to d⁷ ions there is a choice. After three electrons occupy t₂g singly, the fourth can either pair up in t₂g (costing the **pairing energy**, P) or go up to e_g (costing Δₒ).

- **Weak-field ligands** (Δₒ less than P): electrons spread out into e_g first, giving a **high-spin** complex with the most unpaired electrons.
- **Strong-field ligands** (Δₒ greater than P): electrons pair in t₂g first, giving a **low-spin** complex.

Example, Fe²⁺ (d⁶): [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is high spin (t₂g⁴ e_g², 4 unpaired); [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is low spin (t₂g⁶, 0 unpaired). Tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin because Δ is small.

### Magnetism

A complex with unpaired electrons is **paramagnetic** (attracted into a magnetic field). One with all electrons paired is **diamagnetic** (weakly repelled). Measuring magnetism reveals the number of unpaired electrons, n, using the spin-only magnetic moment:

μ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr magnetons (μ_B)

This is a direct experimental test of whether a complex is high spin or low spin.

### Colour

Many transition metal complexes are coloured because an electron can absorb visible light and jump from t₂g to e_g (a **d–d transition**). The energy absorbed equals Δₒ:

Δ = hc ÷ λ

The colour we **see** is the **complementary colour** of the light absorbed. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs mainly orange-red light and appears blue. Changing the ligand changes Δ, so the colour changes: adding ammonia to aqueous Cu²⁺ gives a deeper blue-violet complex because NH₃ is a stronger-field ligand than H₂O, so higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) light is absorbed.

Ions with **d⁰** (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) or **d¹⁰** (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) configurations have no possible d–d transition and are usually **colourless**.

## Worked examples

### Worked example 1: analysing a complex

**Question:** For K₄[Fe(CN)₆], find (a) the oxidation state of Fe, (b) the d-electron count, (c) the coordination number and geometry, (d) the name, and (e) the number of unpaired electrons and magnetic behaviour.

**(a)** Four K⁺ give +4, so the complex ion is [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻. Fe + 6(−1) = −4, so **Fe = +2**.

**(b)** Fe is in group 8: 8 − 2 = **d⁶** ([Ar] 3d⁶).

**(c)** Six monodentate CN⁻ ligands: coordination number **6, octahedral**.

**(d)** The complex is an anion, so the metal ends in -ate using the Latin root: **potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)**.

**(e)** CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand, so the complex is low spin: all six electrons pair in t₂g (t₂g⁶ e_g⁰). **0 unpaired electrons; diamagnetic.**

### Worked example 2: magnetic moment and spin state

**Question:** [CoF₆]³⁻ has a measured magnetic moment of about 4.9 μ_B. Is it high spin or low spin?

**Step 1 — d count.** F⁻ is −1, so Co + 6(−1) = −3, giving Co(+3). Group 9 − 3 = **d⁶**.

**Step 2 — Predict both options.** High spin d⁶: t₂g⁴ e_g², n = 4. Low spin d⁶: t₂g⁶, n = 0.

**Step 3 — Calculate μ for n = 4.** μ = √(4 × (4 + 2)) = √24 = 4.90 μ_B.

**Step 4 — Compare.** The measured value of 4.9 μ_B matches n = 4. The complex is **high spin**, as expected since F⁻ is a weak-field ligand.

### Worked example 3: Δ from the colour of a complex

**Question:** [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs most strongly at λ = 500 nm. Calculate Δₒ in kJ mol⁻¹. (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

**Step 1 — Energy per photon.** E = hc ÷ λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) ÷ (500 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.973 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

**Step 2 — Per mole.** 3.973 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 2.392 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹.

**Step 3 — Units and significant figures.** Δₒ = **239 kJ mol⁻¹** (3 s.f.).

Ti³⁺ is d¹, so this is its single t₂g to e_g transition; absorbing blue-green light makes the solution look purple.

## Common mistakes

- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming ions. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
- Confusing coordination number with the number of ligands. Three en ligands give coordination number 6.
- Saying the colour seen is the colour absorbed. You see the complementary colour.
- Applying high-spin/low-spin choices to d¹–d³ or d⁸–d¹⁰ octahedral ions, where only one arrangement is possible.
- Naming errors: forgetting alphabetical order of ligands, writing "amine" instead of "ammine", or forgetting "-ate" for anionic complexes.

## Exam tips

- For a given formula, work in order: oxidation state, d count, geometry, name, crystal field diagram, unpaired electrons.
- On crystal field diagrams, label t₂g, e_g and Δₒ, and justify the spin state from the spectrochemical series.
- For colour questions, link three ideas: d–d transition, energy absorbed equals Δ, and the observed colour is complementary.
- Calculations with E = hc ÷ λ are marked on units: convert nm to m and remember to multiply by Avogadro's number for a molar value.

## Tips to remember

- **"First in, first out"** — 4s fills first in the atom and empties first in the ion.
- **d count = group number − oxidation state** — the fastest way to the d electrons of any transition metal ion.
- **Spectrochemical series mnemonic** (a made-up memory trick): "**I B**ought **C**heap **F**ancy **O**ranges, **W**ow, **N**ice **E**ating, **C**ool **C**hoice" for I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, en, CN⁻, CO — from weak to strong field.
- **Axis attack picture:** imagine six ligands sitting on the x, y and z axes. The two d orbitals that point at them (z² and x²−y²) get pushed up — those are e_g. The three that dodge between the axes stay low — t₂g.
- **Strong field squeezes in** (a made-up memory trick): strong-field ligands make the gap too big to jump, so electrons squeeze into the lower level and pair up (low spin).
- **No d–d, no colour:** d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) are colourless — check this whenever a question asks about colour.

## Key terms

- **Ligand** — a molecule or ion that donates a lone pair to a central metal.
- **Coordinate (dative) bond** — a covalent bond in which both electrons come from one atom.
- **Coordination number** — the number of donor atoms bonded to the central metal.
- **Chelating ligand** — a ligand with two or more donor atoms that binds the same metal, forming a ring.
- **Chelate effect** — the extra stability of chelate complexes, largely due to increased entropy.
- **Crystal field splitting energy (Δ)** — the energy gap between the split d-orbital sets.
- **Spectrochemical series** — the order of ligands by the size of splitting they cause.
- **High spin / low spin** — maximum or minimum number of unpaired electrons for a given d count.
- **Paramagnetic** — having unpaired electrons and being attracted into a magnetic field.
- **d–d transition** — excitation of an electron between split d orbitals by absorbing visible light.

## Summary

- First-row transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d; the d count of an ion is group number minus oxidation state.
- Variable oxidation states arise because 4s and 3d energies are close; Mn reaches +7.
- Complexes contain ligands bonded by coordinate bonds; coordination numbers 4 and 6 give tetrahedral, square planar and octahedral shapes, with cis–trans and optical isomers possible.
- Names list ligands alphabetically before the metal, with the oxidation state in Roman numerals and -ate for anionic complexes.
- Crystal field theory splits d orbitals into t₂g and e_g; the ligand's field strength decides high or low spin and so the magnetism.
- Colour comes from d–d transitions; the colour seen is complementary to that absorbed, and d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are colourless.

questions.prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the Mn²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; forming Mn²⁺ removes the two 4s electrons first, leaving [Ar] 3d⁵. A is the tempting error of removing 3d electrons first because 4s is filled first. B is the neutral atom.

questions.prompt: What is the coordination number of cobalt in [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺, where en is ethane-1,2-diamine?
questions.explanation: Each en ligand is bidentate and contributes two donor N atoms (4 in total), and each Cl⁻ contributes one (2 in total), so six donor atoms surround cobalt. B is tempting because there are four ligands, but coordination number counts donor atoms, not ligands.

questions.prompt: What is the correct IUPAC name of [Cr(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl?
questions.explanation: The complex cation is [Cr(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺: Cr + 2(−1) = +1, so Cr is +3. Ligands are listed alphabetically ignoring prefixes: ammine before chlorido. The complex is a cation, so no -ate ending. B is tempting but uses -ate, which is only for anionic complexes; C has the wrong oxidation state; A breaks alphabetical order.

questions.prompt: Why is aqueous Zn²⁺ colourless, whereas aqueous Cu²⁺ is blue?

options.A: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so no d–d transition is possible; Cu²⁺ is d⁹ and can absorb visible light by a d–d transition.
options.B: Zn²⁺ does not form complexes with water.
options.C: Zn²⁺ has a larger crystal field splitting that absorbs only ultraviolet light.
options.D: Cu²⁺ emits blue light when its electrons fall back to lower levels.

questions.explanation: A d–d transition needs a vacancy in the higher d level. Zn²⁺ has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell, so no such transition occurs and it is colourless. Cu²⁺ (d⁹) absorbs orange-red light and appears blue. D is tempting but wrong: the colour comes from light absorbed, and we see the complementary colour, not emitted light.

questions.prompt: How many unpaired electrons are present in the low-spin octahedral complex [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺?
questions.explanation: Co³⁺ is d⁶ (group 9 − 3). In a low-spin octahedral complex all six electrons pair in the t₂g set (t₂g⁶ e_g⁰), so there are no unpaired electrons and the complex is diamagnetic. A is tempting because it is the high-spin d⁶ result (t₂g⁴ e_g²), which applies to weak-field ligands.

questions.prompt: Adding excess ammonia to pale blue [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ solution gives a deep blue-violet solution. Which explanation is best?

options.A: NH₃ is a weaker-field ligand than H₂O, so lower-energy light is absorbed.
options.B: NH₃ is a stronger-field ligand than H₂O, so Δₒ increases and shorter-wavelength (higher-energy) light is absorbed.
options.C: NH₃ oxidises Cu²⁺ to Cu³⁺, which has a different colour.
options.D: NH₃ removes the d electrons from copper.

questions.explanation: NH₃ lies above H₂O in the spectrochemical series, so replacing water ligands increases Δₒ and shifts absorption to higher energy (shorter wavelength); the observed complementary colour shifts accordingly. A reverses the order of the spectrochemical series. C is wrong: the oxidation state stays +2.

questions.prompt: A complex absorbs light most strongly at 600 nm. What is the crystal field splitting energy in kJ mol⁻¹? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation: E = hc ÷ λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) ÷ (600 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.311 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon. Multiplying by Nₐ gives 1.994 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ = 199 kJ mol⁻¹. A forgets Avogadro's number (and is in J, not kJ); C forgets to convert J to kJ; B is the value for 500 nm.

questions.prompt: Which complex can exist as cis and trans geometric isomers?
questions.explanation: In square planar [PtCl₂(NH₃)₂], the two Cl ligands can be adjacent (cis, the drug cisplatin) or opposite (trans). A and D have only one kind of ligand, so no isomers are possible. C is tempting, but in a tetrahedron all positions are adjacent to each other, so tetrahedral complexes cannot show cis–trans isomerism.
